title: [Vantage Point] The Legarda-Leviste solar empire: From government contracts to private billions
summary: In renewable energy, the true measure of entrepreneurial success is electricity delivered to the grid—not merely shares sold or paper valuations achieved.

blocks.text: Behind Leandro Leviste’s entrepreneurial success lies a corporate strategy that converted government-awarded development opportunities into marketable equity, generated billions in financial transactions, and left substantial contractual obligations unresolved.

Leandro Leviste was undeniably innovative, though his commercial ingenuity extended well beyond the technology of generating solar power. His corporate strategy demonstrated how exclusive renewable-energy development rights granted by the government could acquire enormous financial value even before some of the projects underpinning them delivered electricity. (READ: Leviste solar companies passed around DOE deals as franchisee incurred losses)
Did the Filipino public receive economic benefits commensurate with the private wealth those state-granted opportunities helped create?

In the first installment, Vantage Point examined the Anti-Money Laundering Council’s (AMLC) allegations concerning Senator Loren Legarda, former Energy secretary Alfonso Cusi, and Leviste in the acquisition and retention of solar development rights.
We now trace what happened after those rights were secured: how corporate assets were consolidated, how shares were monetized, and how billions subsequently moved through Leviste’s personal accounts.

The corporate strategy centered on Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc. (SPPPHI), Leviste’s principal investment vehicle. In February 2022, a reported asset-for-share swap involving interests in 20 solar project companies and associated assets (See list of these companies below this paragraph) was structured around roughly 24.37 billion shares of SP New Energy Corp. (SPNEC), valued at P2.50 apiece. That translated into a transaction valuation of approximately P60.93 billion, subject to the terms and completion of the share exchange. (See list of these companies:

items: Solar Philippines Commercial Rooftop Projects, Inc.

blocks.text: To be clear, this was not P60.93 billion in cash earnings. Still, it illustrates how development rights, corporate interests, and related assets could be packaged into marketable equity capable of attracting institutional capital. A privately held portfolio had found a direct pipeline for monetization through the stock market.

The entry of Meralco PowerGen Corp. (MGen) gave that pipeline substantial financial muscle. In 2023, its renewable-energy arm, MGreen, injected P15.9 billion into newly issued SPNEC shares—capital that flowed directly into the listed company. Subsequent deals involving existing shares and exchangeable financing arrangements, however, provided funding opportunities for Leviste’s corporate vehicles as selling shareholders or borrowers. (READ: Leandro Leviste sells another P3 billion in SPNEC shares as solar controversies mount)

By June 2025, Leviste had announced completed and agreed share transactions totaling P20.49 billion, comprising P18.26 billion involving the MGen group and P2.23 billion from earlier sales to public investors. His widely publicized P34-billion funding target included prospective deals and financing arrangements and should not be mistaken for fully realized personal cash-outs.
SPNEC investment and share transactions

blocks.caption: Source: SPNEC June 25, 2025 PSE clarification. MGen group deals and public sales total P20.49 billion.

blocks.text: Monetization continued even after Leviste entered Congress. On August 20, 2026, SPPPHI offloaded another 2.4 billion SPNEC shares at P1.25 apiece, raising P3 billion in gross proceeds and paring its common-share stake from 16.30% to 11.51%. Eight days later, SPNEC’s board approved the acquisition by its wholly owned subsidiary, Terra Nueva Inc., of land from Provincia Investments Corp. and JJPNM Agro Industrial Corp.—both subsidiaries of SPPPHI.

As Vantage Point previously reported, the land acquisition disclosure omitted the purchase price, acreage, and valuation methodology. While there is no established link between the share sale and the proposed land purchases, minority shareholders deserve full transparency on the terms under which Leviste’s private firms continue transacting with the listed company as his equity stake shrinks.

The AMLC’s financial investigation adds another layer to the picture. According to reported Court of Appeals records, Leviste’s accounts logged roughly P28.07 billion in inflows and P29.82 billion in outflows, representing P57.89 billion in cumulative financial activity. Investigators also flagged 1,044 checks totaling roughly P14.99 billion issued to Leviste by his solar companies, raising concerns about the possible commingling of corporate and personal funds.
Reported financial activity in Leviste’s accounts

blocks.caption: Source: Reported AMLC findings in Court of Appeals proceedings. The P14.99 billion in checks is not added to this total

blocks.text: Here, the accounting principle is fundamental. Corporations have legal personalities distinct from their shareholders. Funds transferred to an owner must rest on a clear accounting and legal basis—whether as dividends, loan repayments, advances, or other legitimate transactions. Owning a corporation does not automatically make its cash the owner’s personal property.

Leviste maintains that all transactions were lawful and undertaken in the ordinary course of business. Assessing that claim requires a line-by-line reconciliation of corporate ledgers, bank statements, tax filings, and underlying contracts. Gross transaction volume alone does not establish unlawful enrichment. (READ: Leviste denies he made money from selling franchise to Pangilinan’s Meralco group)

Meanwhile, major contractual commitments went unmet. The AMLC identified roughly P10.44 billion tied to 26 terminated renewable-energy contracts. Separately, the Department of Energy (DOE) pegged its broader aggregate demands against Solar Philippines, its subsidiaries, and affiliates at P24 billion. Because the two figures cover different scopes and may overlap, they should not be combined—nor do they represent final judicial awards. (READ: DOE: Only 0.3% collected from P24 billion in penalties vs Leviste’s Solar Philippines)

Just as importantly, these reported obligations should not automatically be pinned on today’s SPNEC. Under MGen’s stewardship, MTerra Solar Phase 1 began commercial operations in August 2026, initially declaring 600 MWac under its Meralco power-supply agreement. That represents tangible project delivery, and the capital and execution risks shouldered by the new controlling shareholder deserve due recognition.

blocks.caption: Goodbye, SPNEC: MVP rebrands Leviste’s solar firm, lines up P5-B deal

blocks.text: Similarly, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s inquiry into alleged franchise flipping demands legal precision. Solar Para sa Bayan’s congressional franchise is legally separate from the DOE service contracts held by other Solar Philippines entities, and MGen has denied acquiring shares in the franchise holder. Whether any transaction circumvented statutory restrictions remains a question for investigators to address.

The Court of Appeals’ freeze orders remain provisional safeguards, not convictions. What the government must now establish is straightforward: which corporate entities owe money, where the proceeds of monetization went, and whether the individuals behind unfulfilled obligations can be held legally accountable. (READ: Loren Legarda, Leandro Leviste face plunder, graft complaints over solar projects)

In renewable energy, the true measure of entrepreneurial success is electricity delivered to the grid—not merely shares sold or paper valuations achieved. Government development rights are instruments of national energy policy, not unconditional entitlements to private fortune. Filipinos are owed a transparent accounting of both sides of the ledger: what private enterprise gained from public privileges and what the nation received in return. – Rappler.com

Source note: This analysis draws from reported AMLC findings contained in Court of Appeals proceedings, SPNEC’s Philippine Stock Exchange disclosures and corporate filings, Department of Energy pronouncements, statements from the parties concerned, and previous Vantage Point investigations into Solar Philippines and SPNEC.
